solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Friend from Eastern Europe reported fall of King (9)

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we want the sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: a mate (friend) from the Czech Republic

annotation.surface: A news item about the downfall of a monarch, passed on by a pal from the East.
annotation.walkthrough: Czech and check are pronounced identically, so a Czech mate is heard as the chess term. 'King' is the chess piece, not a ruler.
annotation.definitionFit: Checkmate is the move that brings about the king's defeat, ending a game of chess.

entries.clue: Drinking this, the reverse of cappuccino? (5)

definitions.note: Points at the answer as 'this drink'; the whole clue half-reads as a definition too.

indicators.note: reading the word in reverse runs its letters backwards

annotation.surface: A café customer wondering what the opposite of a frothy coffee would be.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: the opposite of a cappuccino is tea, and a cuppa is tucked backwards into the coffee's own name.
annotation.definitionFit: Cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea, so 'drinking this' points to the tea in hand.

entries.clue: “Sinner” for “sinker”? I’m not sure — “singer”? Let me think (7)

blocks.note: the hesitant noise of someone unsure
one who sings to the police is an informer, a rat

annotation.surface: Someone half-remembering a word, trying one candidate after another.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening quote is the definition by example: printing 'sinner' where 'sinker' was meant is a misprint. The hesitation noises that follow look like surface chatter but are the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: An erratum is an error in print, such as one wrong letter turning 'sinker' into 'sinner'.

entries.clue: Dangerous animal caught, nothing retarding cycles (4,5)

indicators.note: to cycle a string is to rotate it, taking letters from one end round to the other

annotation.surface: A zookeeper's report: a dangerous beast has been captured, with bikes involved somehow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retarding' means slowing, and the turn of the cycle carries the last four letters round to lead off; 'cycles' looks like bicycles in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: The king cobra is the world's longest venomous snake.

entries.clue: Post a couple of applications (11)

blocks.note: an app is a software application
an ointment is an application rubbed on the skin

annotation.surface: Advice on mailing a pair of job forms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Applications' serves twice in different senses: the phone kind (APP) and the medical kind (OINTMENT). 'Post' is a job, not the mail.
annotation.definitionFit: An appointment is a post or position someone has been appointed to.

entries.clue: Periodically, new baby will want a drop of water (3)

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so take every other letter

annotation.surface: A newborn now and again needing a little water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A drop of water' is the tide falling, not a droplet.
annotation.definitionFit: An ebb is the falling of the tide, a drop in the water level.

entries.clue: Part of leg somewhat laid back nurses start to ice (5)

indicators.note: lying back puts the word the other way round
to nurse is to hold close, so it goes round the letter
the start of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A laid-back patient's sore leg being nursed with ice.
annotation.walkthrough: A BIT turned round is TIBA, which then holds the I between B and A.
annotation.definitionFit: The tibia is the shinbone, the larger bone of the lower leg.

entries.clue: Numbers clocked / by / my employer (5)

annotation.surface: A worker listing the figures they logged for the boss.
annotation.walkthrough: A triple definition: 'by' is a third sense squeezed between the other two. The Times is the London newspaper this puzzle comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: Race times are figures clocked, 'times' is the multiplication word for 'by', and The Times publishes this puzzle.

blocks.note: the multiplication sense: three by four is twelve
the setter speaks as the newspaper's employee: the London daily that prints this puzzle

entries.clue: A bit miffed receiving only half as much rice (7)

indicators.note: put out, upset, so the letters are disturbed
one part takes another inside it
keep just half of the phrase's letters

blocks.note: the first three of the six letters of AS MUCH

annotation.surface: Someone a little put out that their portion of rice is half the size.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As much' is the whole six-letter phrase AS MUCH, halved; the surface wants 'only half as much' to be a quantity of rice.
annotation.definitionFit: Basmati is a long-grain aromatic rice from South Asia.

entries.clue: Append residence, look, beneath this? (9)

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation, as in 'res.' on an address

annotation.surface: Instructions for writing an envelope: put the home address under the name.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: on an envelope you add the residence beneath the addressee's name.
annotation.definitionFit: The addressee is the person named on a letter, with their address written underneath.

entries.clue: Root cut, following usual number of strokes (7)

indicators.note: the cut comes after the number of strokes

blocks.note: par is the expected number of golf strokes

annotation.surface: A gardener trimming a root after the usual number of chops.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Strokes' are golf strokes, not blows of a knife.
annotation.definitionFit: A parsnip is eaten for its tap root, so 'root' is a definition by category.

entries.clue: Looking for enlightenment they quickly run through plot (7)

indicators.note: the runners pass through the middle of the plot

blocks.note: a flower bed is a plot

annotation.surface: Seekers after enlightenment rushing about a piece of land.
annotation.walkthrough: 'They quickly run' is a cryptic description of emus, flightless birds that sprint. 'Plot' is a garden bed, not a story.
annotation.definitionFit: Bemused means puzzled, and a puzzled person is seeking enlightenment, so this is a description rather than a synonym.

entries.clue: No place for carriage in mighty caper (5)

indicators.note: the carriage is not allowed to stay in the word, so it is removed

blocks.note: a gig is a light two-wheeled carriage

annotation.surface: A mighty escapade with no room for a coach.
annotation.walkthrough: GIGANTIC without GIG leaves ANTIC.
annotation.definitionFit: An antic is a caper, a playful or absurd piece of behaviour.

entries.clue: I will not run out of highway (9)

definitions.note: Describes the state of a person who has made no will: 'I am intestate' means 'I have no will'.

indicators.note: the run is taken out of the highway

blocks.note: an interstate is an American highway

annotation.surface: A defiant driver refusing to leave the motorway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I will not' reads as a refusal, but 'will' is a legal document: someone with no will dies intestate.
annotation.definitionFit: Intestate is the legal word for dying without a will, so 'I will not' is a cryptic reading of 'I, no will'.

entries.clue: Child’s character we think encapsulates “untrustworthy” (11)

indicators.note: wraps one thing inside another

blocks.note: Jack Reacher is the hero of Lee Child's thrillers

annotation.surface: A parent judging that their offspring's nature is not to be trusted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Child' is the novelist Lee Child, capitalised because it starts the clue; his character is Jack Reacher. TO US wraps REACHER.
annotation.definitionFit: Treacherous means disloyal, not to be trusted.

entries.clue: Priest is missing a beat (3)

indicators.note: the priest's name lacks the letter A

blocks.note: a lama is a Buddhist priest

annotation.surface: A cleric who has lost the rhythm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beat' means thrash, not a musical beat.
annotation.definitionFit: Lam is informal, chiefly British, for thrash or hit hard, a sense of beat.

entries.clue: The method underpinning entries in Crossword Championship spectacle (5,4)

indicators.note: in a down answer, what underpins sits below, so the method comes after

annotation.surface: A contestant describing the technique behind their answers at a solving contest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lights' is solvers' jargon for the answers in a grid; the Times runs an annual Crossword Championship.
annotation.definitionFit: A light show is a spectacle of coloured lights and lasers.

entries.clue: Nervous feeling, say, associated with Burton’s debut theatre part (11)

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so take the first letter

blocks.note: the flies are the space above a stage where scenery hangs

annotation.surface: Stage fright before Richard Burton's first performance in a play.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the actor's first-night nerves, but 'debut' just takes his initial.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Butterflies in the stomach' is the idiom for the fluttering of nerves, shortened here to the one word.

entries.clue: Its influence is Sweet Charity in the setting for Les Misérables (9)

definitions.note: A describing clause for the noun: a fragrance is something whose effect is sweet.

indicators.note: a setting holds a jewel, so one part is placed inside the other

blocks.note: the country where Hugo's novel is set
a rag is a British student charity fund-raising event

annotation.surface: A theatre note: the musical Sweet Charity has influenced a staging of Les Misérables.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals make 'Sweet Charity' look like the musical, but the words split up: 'Sweet' ends the definition and 'Charity' is RAG.
annotation.definitionFit: A fragrance is a scent whose effect on the senses is sweet.

entries.clue: Waterproof, this is instinctive: spill tea! (5-6)

definitions.note: Used as a noun, a waterproof material.

blocks.note: a spill is a thin strip of wood or paper for lighting, a taper
cha (char) is British slang for tea

annotation.surface: Someone reflexively knocking over their tea, glad the table is waterproof.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spill' is a noun here, a lighting taper, not the verb for knocking a drink over.
annotation.definitionFit: Gutta-percha is a waterproof latex from Malaysian trees, once used to insulate undersea cables.

entries.clue: One pushing athlete, European, right to the very south of ground (7)

indicators.note: in a down answer, south means below, so these letters go at the bottom

blocks.note: to ground someone in a subject is to train them in it

annotation.surface: A sports report about a European runner being pushed right to the bottom end of the stadium.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a sports ground but is the verb, as in 'well grounded in maths'.
annotation.definitionFit: A trainer coaches an athlete, pushing them harder in training.

entries.clue: Introduction to Götterdämmerung that surprises me! (3)

indicators.note: the introduction is the first letter

blocks.note: the first letter G, written out as the letter's name

annotation.surface: An opera-goer startled by the opening of Wagner's epic.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is the letter G spelt out as a word, which happens to be the exclamation too.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Gee!' is an exclamation of surprise.

entries.clue: Being divine, cheese is tucked away by girl (7)

definitions.note: Read as 'divine being'; the answer is the name of one.

indicators.note: the cheese is put away inside the girl

annotation.surface: A girl heavenly enough to put away a lot of cheese.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Being divine' looks like an adjective phrase about the girl but inverts to 'divine being'.
annotation.definitionFit: Gabriel is the archangel of the Bible, an example of a divine being.

entries.clue: Unsteadily take aim at Balmoral boiler (3,6)

indicators.note: shakily, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: ettle is a Scots word for aim or intend

annotation.surface: A shaky shot fired at the royal family's Scottish castle.
annotation.walkthrough: Balmoral is the royal estate in Scotland, which signals a Scots word: ETTLE, to aim.
annotation.definitionFit: A boiler is anything that boils water, and a tea kettle is the everyday example.

entries.clue: Eve and Adam finally ran into someone doing the Eden Project? (5)

indicators.note: take the last letter of each word

blocks.note: the last letters of Eve and Adam

annotation.surface: The first couple meeting someone in the Garden of Eden.
annotation.walkthrough: The Eden Project is a big tourist attraction in Cornwall, and emmet is the Cornish word for a tourist. The biblical names are there to point to Eden.
annotation.definitionFit: An emmet is Cornish slang for a tourist, such as a visitor to the Eden Project.

entries.clue: Cryptic pictures on public transport (5)

annotation.surface: Puzzling posters on the side of a bus.
annotation.walkthrough: RE for 'on' is the sense of 'regarding', as in a memo heading.
annotation.definitionFit: A rebus is a puzzle using pictures to represent words.

entries.clue: Ridicule the people here about money (5)

indicators.note: turned about, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to rag is to tease or ridicule

annotation.surface: Locals mocking someone over cash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sugar' as money is dated slang.
annotation.definitionFit: Sugar is dated British slang for cash, like bread or dough.

entries.clue: Chinese agent engaged in Washington diversion (7)

blocks.note: the Han are China's majority people
a G-man is an FBI agent, a US government man

annotation.surface: A spy from China working in the US capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Engaged in Washington' only locates the agent as American; it is not a container instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Hangman is a word-guessing game, a diversion.

entries.clue: Pain / riding horse (3)

annotation.surface: A saddle-sore rider.
annotation.walkthrough: A nag is a pain in the sense of someone who keeps on at you.
annotation.definitionFit: A nag is both a pester, a pain in the neck, and a horse, usually a worn-out one.

blocks.note: someone who keeps on at you is a pain
an old or ordinary horse for riding

entries.clue: Why writer stops working? Good you hear this about pen (7)

blocks.note: O INK IN: nought ink inside, which is why a pen runs dry

annotation.surface: A pen that has run dry, and someone saying it is good to hear about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The writer is the pen, and it stops when it has zero ink in it. The second 'pen' is a pigpen, where the grunting goes on.
annotation.definitionFit: Pigs in a pen make an oinking noise, so it is the sound heard around one.

entries.clue: Counterintuitively best fare from Bavaria — zilch for you in the end (5)

indicators.note: zilch comes in for, in place of, the letter taken from 'you'
the end of a word is its last letter

annotation.surface: A food review: the finest German sausage, but not for you at the end of the day.
annotation.walkthrough: As a verb, to worst someone is to best them, which is why the setter says counterintuitively.
annotation.definitionFit: To worst an opponent means to defeat them, the same as to best them.

entries.clue: Church reader, fast one, keeps time (9)

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so GOER holds SPELL inside

blocks.note: a goer is someone who goes fast
a spell is a period of time

annotation.surface: A church lectern reader who is quick and keeps good time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fast one' suggests a trick or a speedy person; it is GOER.
annotation.definitionFit: A gospeller reads the Gospel aloud in a church service.
